description: Team Obliviate is a multidisciplinary team united by curiosity about how our planet speaks through data. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we combine research, data analysis, programming, design and video storytelling, questioning assumptions and refining ideas until they are clear, useful and easy to experience. We value curiosity, collaboration and the courage to present complex science in new ways, so more people can hear, read and trust Earth’s open data.
summary: EARTHSENSE is an interactive, multi-sensory experience that makes Earth science more accessible by transforming NASA Earth observations into sound, visualizations, and easy-to-understand text explanations. It helps students, educators, researchers, and curious people explore our changing planet through three experiences: Ocean Light → Sound, Earth's Changing Pulse (temperature, sea level, and atmospheric CO₂), and Earth vs Another World. By combining data-driven sonification, synchronized text explanations, interactive visualizations, and a conversational Earth interface, EARTHSENSE  helps users see, hear, read, and better understand the signals of our planet.
details:
EARTHSENSE

Study breakdown: a site that turns NASA data into sound

. The core idea

Earth Sense is an interactive website that lets you hear scientific datasets instead of only reading charts. Each data point becomes one musical note: a higher value gives a higher pitch. The same value is also shown as a color and written out as a plain sentence, so listening and reading never disagree.

Analogy: A stethoscope for the planet. A stethoscope doesn't diagnose anyone. It makes a hidden signal audible so a trained person can notice patterns. Earth Sense does that for ocean pigment, temperature, sea level, lightning and distant starlight, and it keeps a label on every signal saying what it can and cannot tell you.

Home page: "Every signal has a story. Where will you begin?" with a ticker of live-style Earth statistics and three entry cards.

. What is inside

Experience 1: ocean color

Pick a basin, press play, and each month of satellite pigment data becomes a note. A mode switch offers Listen, Read or Both. The December reading for the Bay of Bengal is 0.330 mg/m³, which lands at 83% of the pitch scale and is described as a pigment-rich month tied to river nutrients and monsoon mixing.

Listening studio for the Bay of Bengal: the water's color, haze and drifting plankton all follow the chlorophyll value.

. How the sound is made

The "Read the sound" and "Mapping in plain language" panels spell out the whole method, and it is the most reusable idea on the site:

Normalize: each measurement is scaled to a 0–100% position inside a fixed two-octave pitch window.

One value, one note: order follows the x-axis, so playback is the chart read left to right.

One scale everywhere: chart color and pitch use the same scale, so the picture and the sound agree.

Text from the same number: the written sentence is generated from the normalized value that sets the pitch. "Nothing is added for effect."

"Read the sound" and "The mapping, in plain language" panels, with the source citation below.

Worked examples from the recording:

. Earth's changing pulse

Temperature, sea level and CO₂ are presented as three independent records of one system. The temperature chart runs from −0.60 °C (blue) to +1.4 °C (red) against the 1951–1980 average, and color and pitch share that single scale. Arrow keys step one year at a time. In the globe view, the poles "flush" first because observed warming is amplified there.

Temperature anomaly, 145 yearly observations (1880 onward). Color bar and pitch use the same −0.60 to 1.4 °C scale.

Sea level: 32 yearly observations from satellite altimetry, mapped as millimeters above the 1993 baseline (0–110 mm).

The evidence table under each studio has five rows: source, unit, mapping rule, what it shows, what it cannot show. For sea level it states that radar altimeters measure sea-surface height from orbit, that the rise comes from melting land ice plus thermal expansion, and that the global mean hides regional differences and the satellite record starts only in 1993.

"Evidence and how the sound is made": the site lists its own limits next to the source link.

. Lightning across worlds

A rotating 3D globe marks catalogued lightning hotspots. Layers can be toggled (lightning, day/night, city lights, land) and each storm has a "Hear this storm" button. Headline figures: about 44 flashes per second worldwide and about 1.4 billion per year. As a check, 44 × 31.5 million seconds per year is about 1.39 billion, so the two numbers agree.

Lake Maracaibo selected: 233 flashes per km² per year, peak season September–October.

Six of the ten catalogued hotspots were visible in the recording.

"Four worlds, four levels of certainty." This is the cleverest honesty device on the site. Each world carries a status badge:

Four worlds, four levels of certainty, with source links to NASA Earth Observatory, ISS LIS, Juno and Cassini.

. Exoplanet transits

A planet crossing its star blocks a tiny fraction of the light. The site shows that dip as a falling light curve and plays it as falling pitch. Earth is the reference world, because it is the only one where we already know what the light means. Other worlds are interpreted by comparison.

Earth as the reference world: the silhouette is the planet, the falling light is the sound. Sizes are exaggerated (dimming drawn ×5,008).

 Measured-style light curve: noise around the baseline, with a clear dip during the crossing. A Measured / Model toggle switches to the clean fitted curve.

Three boxes sum up the limits: what light gives us (radius, orbital period and distance, solid versus atmosphere), what it cannot give us (a picture, since a dip is a shadow), and where the sound stops (sonification makes a signal audible, not truer).

. Talk to Earth

A chat panel with five suggested questions, such as "What are your oceans telling us?", "What does this sound mean?" and "What can one measurement not tell us?". It is labelled a guided demonstration built from the site's own datasets, not a general model and not connected to the web. Every reply is drawn from an observation already loaded.

Talk to Earth. A question outside the loaded data returns a polite boundary message instead of an invented answer.

. Design principles

The About page states three commitments, which work as the site's methodology:

Never invent a signal. Every note comes from a published value, the mapping is documented, and the source is one click away.

Say what it cannot show. Each studio names its own limits: clouds, single casts, sparse stations, tentative molecular detections.

Sound is not the only door. Listen, Read or Both, captions, keyboard control and a global mute make it usable by more people.

About page: "Scientific honesty over spectacle."

An "Open data, cited everywhere" section lists NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 (global surface temperature anomalies, 1880 to present) and NOAA GML Mauna Loa CO₂, among others.

. Where it is weak

Snapshots, not live data. The site says its series are embedded snapshots of published records "used here for demonstration". The scrolling ticker and "Earth simulation · live" badge can read as live feeds, which they are not.

The exoplanet curves are reconstructions. The footnote says the light curves are reconstructions with a stated noise floor, not raw photometry, and that orbital parameters are rounded catalogue values. Yet the on-screen label says "Measured curve". For Earth, no measurement from outside exists at all.

Percent-of-scale hides magnitude. "83% of the pitch scale" depends on where the window's ends are set. Fixed per dataset, it makes datasets comparable only in shape, not in size. A listener cannot tell whether 22% is a small or large departure.

Chlorophyll is a monthly average, not a year. The source is labelled as Bay of Bengal climatology, so the twelve notes are a typical seasonal cycle and not one particular year.

Talk to Earth has narrow coverage. In the recording, clicking the suggested question "Why is atmospheric CO₂ changing?" produced the generic "I can only answer from the observations loaded" message. A suggested prompt that cannot be answered undercuts the demo.

No evidence of listener testing. Nothing in the recording shows that people actually understand data better by ear. Pitch is the only sound dimension mapped, and the benefit is assumed rather than measured.

Small, low-contrast captions. Much of the explanatory text is small grey type on near-black, which works against the accessibility goal.

. Verdict

A strong example of honest science communication. Its real contribution is not the sound but the discipline around it: one normalized value drives pitch, color and text; each studio lists source, unit, rule, what it shows and what it cannot; and the lightning page grades certainty across four worlds. The main gaps are validation (no evidence listeners learn from it) and a few labels that blur measured, modelled and reconstructed data.

Reusable pattern: "source → unit → mapping rule → what it shows → what it cannot show." It would work for any data story, including a security or ML one, where the limits of a model are as important as its outputs.
